title: Upper Respiratory Tract: Nose, Sinuses, Pharynx, and Larynx
subject: Respiratory System (RESP)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter covers the anatomy of the upper airway: the nasal cavity and where each paranasal sinus drains, the blood supply that explains nosebleeds, the three levels of the pharynx with their lymphoid tissue and eustachian tube openings, and the cartilages, muscles, and nerves of the larynx. Board questions use this anatomy to explain sinusitis, epistaxis, otitis media from enlarged adenoids, hoarseness, stridor, and aspiration. If you know where each opening sits, which vessel supplies each region, and which nerve senses or moves each part of the larynx, you can reason from a symptom back to the structure involved.
prerequisites: Bones of the skull and face: maxilla, ethmoid, sphenoid, frontal, palatine
Branches of the external and internal carotid arteries
Course of the vagus nerve and the divisions of the trigeminal nerve
Pharyngeal arch derivatives and aortic arch development

connections.how: The larynx protects the trachea and bronchi, and failure of laryngeal sensation sends aspirated material into the dependent bronchopulmonary segments.
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch, so an aortic aneurysm or an enlarged left atrium can cause hoarseness.
The external laryngeal nerve runs with the superior thyroid artery and the recurrent nerve near the inferior thyroid artery, which places both at risk in thyroid disease and surgery.
Waldeyer ring is mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue that samples inhaled and swallowed antigens and enlarges with repeated childhood exposure.
Sinusitis, orbital spread of infection, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, and angiofibroma are all explained by the anatomical relations in this chapter.

terms.def: A curved shelf of bone covered by mucosa that projects from the lateral nasal wall and increases the surface for warming, humidifying, and filtering air.
The air passage lying beneath and lateral to each concha, into which sinuses and the nasolacrimal duct open.
A curved groove in the middle meatus that receives the openings of the frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoid sinuses.
The opening through which a paranasal sinus drains into the nasal cavity.
Removal of trapped particles and microbes by a mucus layer moved along by coordinated beating of cilia toward the sinus ostia and the pharynx.
The anteroinferior part of the nasal septum where several arteries from both carotid systems anastomose; the source of most nosebleeds.
The ring of lymphoid tissue (pharyngeal, tubal, palatine, and lingual tonsils) surrounding the entrances to the airway and digestive tract.
The auditory (eustachian) tube linking the middle ear to the nasopharynx, which equalizes middle ear pressure and drains middle ear secretions.
The opening between the vocal folds and the arytenoid cartilages, the narrowest part of the adult laryngeal airway.
Movement of the vocal folds away from the midline, which opens the glottis for breathing.
The vagal branch that loops back up to the larynx to supply all intrinsic laryngeal muscles except cricothyroid and the mucosa below the vocal folds.
Entry of food, liquid, or secretions into the airway below the vocal folds.

sections.title: Nasal conchae, meatuses, and sinus drainage

blocks.text: The nasal cavity is divided by the septum into two chambers that open in front through the nares and behind through the choanae into the nasopharynx. Each lateral wall carries three conchae (turbinates). The superior and middle conchae are parts of the ethmoid bone, and the inferior concha is a separate bone. The space beneath and lateral to each concha is its meatus, and the narrow space above the superior concha is the sphenoethmoidal recess. The olfactory region covers the roof, the upper septum, and the superior concha; the rest is lined by respiratory epithelium, pseudostratified ciliated columnar cells with goblet cells over a richly vascular lamina propria.

The conchae turn the nasal airstream into thin, turbulent sheets that pass close to warm, moist mucosa. Inspired air is warmed and humidified, and particles are thrown against the mucus layer. Cilia sweep this mucus back toward the nasopharynx to be swallowed, and inside each sinus they beat toward its natural ostium.
Where each sinus opens

The paranasal sinuses are air spaces in the frontal, maxillary, ethmoid, and sphenoid bones, lined by the same respiratory mucosa. Most sinus drainage clusters in the middle meatus. There, the ethmoidal bulla (a bulge formed by middle ethmoid cells) sits above a curved groove, the semilunar hiatus, which leads forward into a channel called the ethmoidal infundibulum. The frontal sinus drains through the frontonasal duct into the infundibulum or the front of the hiatus, the anterior ethmoid cells open into the infundibulum, and the maxillary sinus opens into the back of the hiatus. This shared drainage region is called the ostiomeatal complex. Swelling here can block the frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoid sinuses at once, which is why sinusitis often involves several sinuses on one side.

blocks.title: Drainage of the paranasal sinuses and nasolacrimal duct
rows: Middle meatus (frontonasal duct to the infundibulum or semilunar hiatus)
Anterior cranial fossa behind its thin posterior wall
Orbit above, upper molar roots below (C02)
Pituitary above, cavernous sinus and internal carotid artery laterally, optic nerve superolaterally

blocks.caption: Only the posterior ethmoid cells, the sphenoid sinus, and the nasolacrimal duct use openings outside the middle meatus.

blocks.text: The nasolacrimal duct explains why crying produces a runny nose: tears drain from the medial corner of the eye into the inferior meatus. The relations in the table predict complications. The ethmoid cells are separated from the orbit by the paper-thin lamina papyracea and by valveless veins, so ethmoid sinusitis is the most common source of orbital cellulitis, especially in children. Sphenoid disease can reach the cavernous sinus and optic nerve, and the frontal sinus can spread infection to the frontal bone and anterior cranial fossa. Sinus pain follows trigeminal innervation: frontal and ethmoid sinuses through branches of the ophthalmic division (V1), the maxillary sinus through the maxillary division (V2).

blocks.predict: A patient has swelling of the mucosa confined to the middle meatus. Which sinuses will fail to drain, and which will keep draining?
blocks.explain: The frontal, maxillary, and anterior and middle ethmoid sinuses share the middle meatus and will be blocked; the posterior ethmoid cells (superior meatus) and the sphenoid sinus (sphenoethmoidal recess) open elsewhere.

sections.title: The maxillary sinus and odontogenic sinusitis

blocks.text: The maxillary sinus is the largest paranasal sinus and occupies the body of the maxilla. It is shaped like a pyramid: its base is the lateral wall of the nasal cavity, its roof is the floor of the orbit (with the infraorbital nerve running in a canal within it), and its floor is the alveolar process of the maxilla. It is also the sinus most often infected, and its anatomy explains why.
Why drainage fails

The maxillary ostium lies high on the medial wall, near the roof of the sinus. In an upright person, secretions pooled on the floor cannot run out by gravity; cilia must carry them up the walls and out through the ostium. Drainage therefore depends entirely on working cilia, normal mucus, and an open ostium. The ostium is also narrow and opens into the crowded middle meatus, so the mucosal swelling of a viral cold or allergic rhinitis easily closes it. Trapped secretions lose oxygen, ciliary beating slows, and bacteria that normally colonize the nasopharynx multiply in the retained fluid. In community-acquired disease these are mainly Streptococcus pneumoniae, nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae, and Moraxella catarrhalis, although most acute sinusitis is viral and resolves without bacterial infection.

blocks.title: Acute maxillary sinusitis
steps: Viral rhinitis or allergy swells middle meatus mucosa
Swelling closes the high maxillary ostium
Secretions pool on the sinus floor
Low oxygen slows ciliary clearance
Bacteria multiply in retained fluid
Facial pressure, purulent discharge, upper tooth pain
blocks.caption: Obstruction of the ostium, not the presence of bacteria, starts the process.

blocks.text: Anything that impairs clearance raises the risk. In cystic fibrosis, defective CFTR chloride transport dehydrates mucus so cilia cannot move it. In primary ciliary dyskinesia, defective dynein arms leave cilia immotile or poorly coordinated, giving chronic sinusitis, bronchiectasis, and infertility, with situs inversus in about half of patients (Kartagener syndrome).
The teeth and the sinus floor

The roots of the maxillary molars, and often the second premolar, lie directly beneath the sinus floor. The bone between them may be very thin, and in some people the root tips project into the sinus covered only by mucosa. A periapical abscess can therefore spread upward into the sinus, and an extraction, a displaced root fragment, or a dental implant can open a communication between the mouth and the sinus. The result is odontogenic sinusitis, which is typically unilateral, often foul smelling, and caused by mixed oral flora including anaerobes rather than the usual respiratory pathogens.

Shared nerves link the two sites in both directions. The superior alveolar nerves, branches of V2, supply both the upper teeth and the sinus lining, so maxillary sinusitis is commonly felt as aching in the upper teeth, and a dental infection can be felt as sinus pressure. A unilateral sinusitis that does not behave like an ordinary viral or bacterial episode should prompt a look at the teeth on that side.

sections.title: Kiesselbach area and the sources of epistaxis

blocks.text: The nasal septum receives blood from both the internal and external carotid systems. In the anteroinferior part of the septum, just inside the nostril, several of these arteries anastomose in a dense plexus called Kiesselbach area (also called Little area).

blocks.title: Arteries that anastomose in Kiesselbach area
rows: Descending palatine branch of the maxillary artery
Septal branch of the superior labial
blocks.caption: Because the anterior ethmoidal artery comes from the internal carotid, the area is fed from both carotid systems.

blocks.text: Kiesselbach area bleeds easily for three reasons. The vessels converge in thin mucosa tightly applied to septal cartilage, with little supporting tissue. The area lies directly in the inspired airstream, so dry, cold air cracks the surface and forms crusts. It is also within reach of a finger, and nose picking is the most common cause of anterior bleeding in children. Rhinitis, a deviated septum, and topical irritants add to these factors, while thrombocytopenia, von Willebrand disease, anticoagulants, and hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia (fragile dilated vessels from defects in endoglin or ALK1 signaling) make bleeding more frequent or prolonged.
About 90 percent of nosebleeds are anterior and arise here. They are usually mild, flow mainly out of the nostril, and can be seen on anterior inspection.
Posterior epistaxis

Posterior bleeding arises from branches of the sphenopalatine artery on the posterior septum and lateral wall, deep in the cavity behind the reach of external pressure. These vessels are larger, so bleeding is heavier and often bilateral, and much of the blood runs into the nasopharynx and is swallowed. Swallowed blood can cause nausea, vomiting of blood, dark stools, and an elevated blood urea nitrogen from digested protein. Posterior bleeds occur more often in older adults, in whom atherosclerotic vessels contract poorly after injury, and are associated with hypertension and anticoagulant use. In an adolescent male with recurrent heavy epistaxis and nasal obstruction, consider juvenile nasopharyngeal angiofibroma, a benign but highly vascular tumor near the sphenopalatine foramen.

blocks.title: Anterior versus posterior epistaxis
rows: Older adult, often with vascular disease or on anticoagulants
Down the pharynx, often both sides
blocks.caption: Vessel size and depth decide how heavy the bleed is and where blood goes.

sections.title: Pharynx, Waldeyer ring, and the pharyngotympanic tube

blocks.text: The pharynx is a fibromuscular tube, about 15 cm long, shared by air and food. It runs from the base of the skull to the lower border of the cricoid cartilage at about the level of C6, where it becomes the esophagus. The soft palate and the epiglottis divide it into three levels.

blocks.title: The three levels of the pharynx
rows: Base of skull to soft palate
Adenoids, pharyngotympanic tube openings, tubal tonsils
Soft palate to upper border of epiglottis
Upper border of the epiglottis to the lower border of the cricoid (about C6)
Laryngeal inlet; piriform recesses on each side
blocks.caption: Squamous epithelium lines the levels that food passes through; the nasopharynx carries only air.

blocks.text: The piriform recesses beside the laryngeal inlet channel swallowed material around the larynx, which is why fish bones lodge there. The internal laryngeal nerve runs beneath their mucosa (C06).
Waldeyer ring

Lymphoid tissue surrounds the entrances to the airway and gut: the pharyngeal tonsil on the roof and posterior wall of the nasopharynx, the tubal tonsils around the tube openings, the palatine tonsils, and the lingual tonsil. Like other mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue, the tonsils have no afferent lymphatics; they sample antigens directly from the surface. The palatine tonsils have deep crypts lined by stratified squamous epithelium, while the pharyngeal tonsil is covered by respiratory epithelium thrown into folds. The tissue enlarges through early childhood with repeated antigen exposure and regresses in adolescence.
The pharyngotympanic tube

The pharyngotympanic (eustachian) tube opens on the lateral wall of the nasopharynx, behind the inferior concha, beneath a cartilaginous ridge (torus tubarius). Its lateral third is bony and its medial two thirds cartilaginous. It is closed at rest and opened briefly during swallowing and yawning, mainly by tensor veli palatini, which ventilates the middle ear and lets it drain. In young children the tube is shorter, wider, and more horizontal, so nasopharyngeal secretions and pathogens reach the middle ear easily. In cleft palate the palatal muscles open the tube poorly, so effusions are common.

Enlarged adenoids cause predictable problems. Blocking the choanae forces mouth breathing, gives a hyponasal voice, and causes snoring and sometimes obstructive sleep apnea. Blocking or inflaming the tube openings stops middle ear ventilation, and the adenoids can act as a bacterial reservoir for acute otitis media. Because adenoids normally regress, a new unilateral middle ear effusion in an adult suggests a mass in the nasopharynx, such as nasopharyngeal carcinoma, an Epstein-Barr virus associated tumor that often arises in the pharyngeal recess beside the tube opening.

blocks.title: Enlarged adenoids to otitis media with effusion
steps: Adenoids enlarge and block the tube opening
Middle ear can no longer be ventilated
Mucosa absorbs trapped middle ear gas
Middle ear pressure becomes negative
Fluid is drawn into the middle ear
Damped eardrum movement: conductive hearing loss
blocks.caption: Otitis media with effusion can follow failed ventilation alone, without infection.

blocks.title: Worked example: a child who snores and does not listen
blocks.text: A 5-year-old snores loudly, sleeps with the mouth open, and has a hyponasal voice. Teachers report inattention, and the tympanic membranes are dull and retracted with reduced mobility. Hyponasal speech means something blocks the choanae, and in a child that is usually the pharyngeal tonsil. The same tissue sits beside the pharyngotympanic tube openings. With the tubes blocked, middle ear gas is absorbed, the eardrum is pulled inward (retracted), and fluid fills the middle ear. Fluid damps sound transmission, so a conductive hearing loss looks like inattention.

sections.title: Laryngeal cartilages, intrinsic muscles, and recurrent laryngeal nerve injury

blocks.text: The larynx guards the lower airway and produces voice. Its framework is three unpaired and three paired cartilages. The thyroid cartilage forms the laryngeal prominence; its inferior horns articulate with the cricoid at the cricothyroid joints. The cricoid, at about C6, is shaped like a signet ring and is the only complete cartilaginous ring of the airway. The epiglottis is elastic cartilage that folds over the inlet during swallowing. The paired arytenoids sit on the upper border of the cricoid lamina; each has a vocal process in front, where the vocal ligament attaches, and a muscular process laterally, where muscles pull. The corniculate and cuneiform cartilages are small nodules in the aryepiglottic folds.

The vocal folds run from the vocal processes to the back of the thyroid angle, covered by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium that withstands constant contact; above them lie the vestibular (false) folds. Every movement of the folds comes from the arytenoids rotating and sliding on the cricoid, or from the thyroid tilting on the cricoid.

blocks.title: Intrinsic muscles of the larynx
cols: Action on the arytenoids or thyroid
rows: Pulls muscular process backward, rotating vocal processes outward
Abducts (opens the glottis); the only abductor
Pulls muscular process forward, rotating vocal processes inward
Shortens and relaxes the folds; vocalis fine-tunes tension
Tilts thyroid cartilage forward on the cricoid
Lengthens and tenses the folds, raising pitch
blocks.caption: One muscle opens the glottis, one tenses the folds, and the rest close or relax them.

blocks.text: Because the posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor, losing it leaves the fold unable to move outward. The recurrent laryngeal nerve supplies it and all the adductors, so recurrent nerve injury leaves the fold motionless near the midline (the paramedian position). With one side paralyzed, the folds cannot meet firmly, air escapes during phonation, and the voice becomes hoarse and breathy, with a weak cough. With both sides paralyzed, both folds sit near the midline: the voice may be fairly preserved, but the airway is narrowed, causing inspiratory stridor and possible airway obstruction.
Why the left nerve is vulnerable

The recurrent nerves hook under arteries derived from the embryonic aortic arches. On the right, the distal sixth arch artery regresses, so the nerve moves up to hook under the right subclavian artery (fourth arch) at the root of the neck. On the left, the sixth arch persists as the ductus arteriosus, so the nerve hooks under the aortic arch beside the ligamentum arteriosum and has a long intrathoracic course. Both nerves then ascend in the tracheoesophageal groove, pass close to the inferior thyroid artery, and enter the larynx behind the cricothyroid joint.

blocks.title: Course of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve
steps: Left vagus crosses the aortic arch
Recurrent branch hooks under the arch beside the ligamentum arteriosum
Ascends in the left tracheoesophageal groove
Passes near the inferior thyroid artery behind the thyroid
Enters the larynx behind the cricothyroid joint
Supplies all intrinsic muscles except cricothyroid
blocks.caption: Each point on this course can be compressed or injured.

blocks.text: Thoracic disease therefore affects the left nerve: aortic arch aneurysm, a left hilar or upper lobe lung tumor, mediastinal lymph nodes, and a markedly enlarged left atrium in mitral stenosis. Thyroid surgery or tumors can injure either nerve.

blocks.predict: A patient with long-standing mitral stenosis develops a hoarse voice. Which nerve is affected, and why the left rather than the right?
blocks.explain: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve, which hooks under the aortic arch and runs through the mediastinum near the left atrium; the right nerve turns under the subclavian artery in the neck.
blocks.check: Compare with the course of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.

sections.title: Sensory and motor innervation of the larynx and aspiration

blocks.text: All laryngeal nerves come from the vagus. The superior laryngeal nerve arises high in the neck and divides into internal and external branches; the recurrent laryngeal nerve arises lower. The vocal folds are the dividing line for sensation.

blocks.title: Laryngeal nerves and the result of injury
rows: Mucosa above the vocal folds, including the laryngeal inlet and piriform recesses
Loss of supraglottic sensation and protective reflexes; silent aspiration
Cricothyroid (and part of the inferior constrictor)
Cannot raise pitch; monotonous voice that tires easily
blocks.caption: Sensation divides at the vocal folds; motor supply divides at the cricothyroid.

blocks.text: The internal laryngeal nerve pierces the thyrohyoid membrane with the superior laryngeal artery and runs under the mucosa of the piriform recess. The external laryngeal nerve descends on the inferior pharyngeal constrictor beside the superior thyroid artery, where it can be injured when that artery is tied during thyroid surgery. Its loss leaves the cricothyroid unable to tense the fold, so the voice is weak, monotonous, and cannot reach high notes, although the airway and the fold position remain normal.
Why supraglottic sensation protects the airway

The mucosa above the folds is the airway's alarm system. When food or secretions touch it, internal laryngeal afferents carry the signal to the nucleus of the solitary tract, and motor fibers from the nucleus ambiguus travel in the recurrent laryngeal nerve to close the glottis (the laryngeal adductor reflex) and, together with the respiratory muscles, produce a cough. If supraglottic sensation is lost, material can spill across the inlet and through the glottis without triggering closure or coughing. This silent aspiration leads to aspiration pneumonia, typically in the dependent segments of the right lung, since the right main bronchus is wider, shorter, and more vertical.

blocks.title: Protective reflex of the supraglottic larynx
steps: Bolus or secretions touch supraglottic mucosa
Internal laryngeal afferents fire
Nucleus of the solitary tract in the medulla
Nucleus ambiguus activates recurrent laryngeal motor fibers
Glottis closes and cough expels the material
blocks.caption: Cutting the afferent limb removes the reflex even when the motor nerves are intact.

blocks.text: The level of a lesion predicts the findings. A recurrent nerve lesion causes hoarseness with intact supraglottic sensation. A lesion of the vagus above the origin of the superior laryngeal nerve, as at the jugular foramen or in a lateral medullary infarct involving the nucleus ambiguus and the nucleus of the solitary tract, combines fold paralysis, loss of supraglottic sensation, and loss of cricothyroid tension, together with dysphagia and deviation of the uvula away from the lesion. Because such patients cannot close the glottis or sense the inlet, they are at greatest risk of aspiration.

blocks.title: Worked example: localizing a vagal lesion
blocks.text: After a thyroidectomy, patient A has a breathy, hoarse voice but swallows without coughing or choking. Patient B has a normal speaking voice but cannot sing high notes. Patient C, after a brainstem stroke, is hoarse, coughs weakly, and develops right lower lobe pneumonia. Patient A has a recurrent laryngeal injury: an adductor-weak fold that cannot close firmly, but intact sensation above it. Patient B has lost the external laryngeal nerve and so cricothyroid tension alone. Patient C has a medullary lesion of the nucleus ambiguus and the nucleus of the solitary tract, above every laryngeal branch, so fold movement and protective reflexes fail together, and aspirated material falls into the right lower lobe.

integration.text: Embryology and anatomy explain the clinical patterns. The paranasal sinuses grow as outpouchings of the nasal cavity, so their ostia drain into the meatuses and their mucosa shares the defenses and diseases of the nose. The laryngeal cartilages and muscles derive from the fourth and sixth pharyngeal arches, which is why their nerves are vagal, and the remodeling of the aortic arches places the left recurrent nerve in the chest. Respiratory epithelium, mucociliary transport, and mucosal lymphoid tissue tie the upper airway to cell biology, genetics (CFTR, dynein), and immunology.

Pathology follows obstruction, vascular anatomy, and nerve course. Obstruction of a small opening, whether a sinus ostium or a pharyngotympanic tube, turns a ventilated space into a stagnant one. Bleeding depends on vessel size and position more than on cause. Hoarseness, stridor, loss of pitch, and silent aspiration each localize a lesion along the vagus. The limits are that drainage patterns and sinus sizes vary between people, sinus and tube disease often overlap with allergy and infection, and imaging or endoscopy, not anatomy alone, confirms the site.

summary: The frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoid sinuses drain to the middle meatus; posterior ethmoid cells to the superior meatus; the sphenoid to the sphenoethmoidal recess; the nasolacrimal duct to the inferior meatus.
Swelling of the ostiomeatal complex blocks several sinuses at once, and thin bony walls let ethmoid infection reach the orbit and sphenoid infection reach the cavernous sinus.
The maxillary sinus is most often infected because its ostium is high on the medial wall, so drainage depends entirely on cilia and an open ostium.

Maxillary molar roots lie under the sinus floor, so dental infection or extraction causes unilateral odontogenic sinusitis with mixed oral and anaerobic flora, and V2 refers pain between teeth and sinus.
About 90 percent of nosebleeds arise in Kiesselbach area, fed by sphenopalatine, anterior ethmoidal, greater palatine, and superior labial branches from both carotid systems.
Posterior epistaxis comes from sphenopalatine branches, is heavier, drains into the pharynx, and cannot be reached by external pressure.
Enlarged adenoids block the choanae (mouth breathing, snoring) and the pharyngotympanic tubes (negative middle ear pressure, effusion, conductive hearing loss).
The posterior cricoarytenoid is the only abductor; recurrent nerve injury leaves the fold paramedian, causing hoarseness if unilateral and stridor if bilateral.
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve hooks under the aortic arch, so aneurysm, lung tumor, nodes, or an enlarged left atrium cause left-sided hoarseness.
Internal laryngeal loss removes supraglottic sensation and causes silent aspiration; external laryngeal loss removes cricothyroid tension and high pitch.

verify: Arteries of Kiesselbach area: most review sources list four (sphenopalatine, anterior ethmoidal, greater palatine, superior labial); some anatomy texts also include the posterior ethmoidal artery. Confirm the list NABNE expects.
The share of maxillary sinusitis that is odontogenic is quoted from about 10 percent in older sources to 25 to 40 percent in recent series; no figure is stated here.
The 90 percent anterior and 10 percent posterior split of epistaxis is a consensus estimate; the role of hypertension in posterior epistaxis is debated.
Position of a paralyzed vocal fold after recurrent nerve injury is described as paramedian in most texts and intermediate in some.
Confirm whether NABNE expects the eponyms Kiesselbach, Waldeyer, Kartagener, and Ortner syndrome (hoarseness from an enlarged left atrium), or only the descriptive terms.
Pharynx length (about 15 cm) and the age at which adenoids peak and regress vary slightly between sources.
A nonrecurrent right laryngeal nerve occurs with an aberrant right subclavian artery; it is an exception not covered here if NABNE tests it.
